title_en: Fragments on the Letter to the Romans
author: Didymus the Blind
occasion: Didymus comments on Romans 7 to explain how Paul's anguished first-person statements about sin and the flesh should be understood. He argues that Paul speaks in a borrowed persona to convict those who love sin, not as a description of his own or any baptized believer's condition.
argument: Didymus argues that Paul's words in Romans 7 about the wretched man and indwelling sin are spoken in a substituted persona, not about Paul himself or any Christian buried with Christ in baptism. The 'flesh,' 'sin,' 'law,' and 'death' that enslave are names for the devil, not for the body or God's law. The commandment and law are holy, just, and good; sin, meaning the devil, used the commandment as an occasion to deceive Adam. Since the devil is not sin by nature but became sin, he can become sinful beyond measure, while the body is not evil by nature; the indwelling devil, not the flesh, produces evil.

outline.move: Didymus introduces the principle that Paul speaks in a substituted persona in Romans 7, and that 'flesh,' 'sin,' 'law,' and 'death' can name the devil rather than the body or God's law.

He explains that the persona's words do not fit Paul or any baptized believer, since they have been freed from the flesh named as sin, and begins a brief commentary on the persona's words, starting with sin using the commandment to deceive.
He defends the goodness of the law and commandment, argues that sin is the devil who became sinful beyond measure, and interprets 'nothing good dwells in me' as spoken in Adam's person.
He argues that the body is not evil by nature, that the indwelling devil is the real agent of evil, and that the devil prepares the pattern of sin in the soul as a co-worker with the negligent will.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle whose words in Romans 7 Didymus is interpreting.

cast.name: Adam
cast.who: The first human, whose disobedience brought death and whose person Didymus sees in part of Romans 7.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The Son of God, whose obedience and death free believers from sin and death.

cast.name: the devil
cast.who: The originator and father of sins, called 'sin,' 'flesh,' 'law,' and 'death' in Scripture.

cast.name: Judas
cast.who: The disciple into whose heart Satan entered, cited as an example of the devil dwelling in a person.

cast.name: Ananias
cast.who: The man whose heart Satan filled, cited as an example of the devil dwelling in a person.

voices.speaker: Paul (in a substituted persona)
voices.how_marked: Didymus says Paul speaks 'in a substituted persona' (ἐν παρενθέτῳ προσώπῳ) and by 'personification' (προσωποποιΐα); the quoted words are from Romans 7.

voices.speaker: Adam (as the person behind a specific Pauline statement)
voices.how_marked: Didymus states that Paul 'now explains into the person of Adam' (εἰς τὸ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ πρόσωπον ἐξηγεῖται) regarding the statement 'I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh.'

voices.speaker: the devil (reported deceptive speech)
voices.how_marked: Didymus introduces the devil's deceptive argument with 'he says' (φησίν), but the quoted words that follow are a distorted version of God's command, embedded within Didymus's narrative of the deception.

voices.speaker: the impious (hypothetical objectors)
voices.how_marked: Didymus says 'I will speak according to the impious' (κατὰ τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς ἐρῶ).

key_terms.sense: In this work, when used negatively, a name for the devil or the condition of enslavement to him, not the physical body itself.
Personified as the devil, the originator and father of sins, not merely individual sinful acts.
Can mean God's holy law, or, when opposed to the law of the mind, the devil's enslaving power.
Both physical death and the spiritual death of disobedience that reigned before Christ.
The rhetorical device by which Paul speaks in the character of another person, here Adam or the unregenerate person.
A substituted or inserted persona, the borrowed character in which Paul speaks.
Adam's disobedience, which brought death and enslavement to the devil.
The condemnation from which those in Christ Jesus are freed.
The commandment given to Adam, which is holy, just, and good, though the devil used it as an occasion for deception.
To work out or produce something fully; Didymus distinguishes the devil's preparatory 'working out' of sin from the completed act.
To dwell in; used of Christ dwelling in the righteous and the devil dwelling in evildoers.
The soul's power of self-determination, able to incline toward whatever actions it chooses.

scripture: Didymus quotes from the Septuagint and Paul's letters. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint. In modern citation, use standard English Bible book names and note where Septuagint numbering differs from the Hebrew.
uncertain: The exact date of composition of these fragments.
The original addressee or immediate audience of the commentary.
Whether the fragments come from a continuous commentary or from catena excerpts.

_unresolved_facts.claim: the devil (reported deceptive speech) ... Didymus introduces the devil's deceptive argument with 'he says' (φησίν), but the quoted words that follow are a distorted version of God's command, embedded within Didymus's narrative of the deception.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἔστι δὲ αὕτη· τί ὅτι, φησίν, εἶπεν ὁ θεός· ἀπὸ παντὸς ξύλου τοῦ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ οὐ φάγεσθε βρώσει; καὶ ᾗ δ' ἂν ἡμέρᾳ φάγησθε ἀπ' αὐτοῦ, διανοιχθήσονται ὑμῶν οἱ ὀφθαλμοί, καὶ ἔσεσθε ὡς θεοί, γινώσκοντες καλὸν καὶ πονηρόν. σοφίζεται δὲ αὐτοὺς μείζονι ἐπαγγελίᾳ κατακρύψαι τὴν ἀπάτην
_unresolved_facts.fix: The φησίν introduces the serpent's words to Eve (with 'he says' referring to the devil/serpent speaking), not a 'distorted version of God's command' as an embedded narrative. The devil quotes God's command and then adds his own deceptive promise ('you will be as gods'). The voice is the devil speaking directly to Eve, not merely 'reported deceptive speech' embedded in narrative.

The substituted persona (προσωποποιΐα) is explicitly discussed in u01-open and u01-rem-early, but in u01-rem-mid and u01-rem-close, Didymus shifts to interpreting specific statements as spoken 'in the person of Adam' (εἰς τὸ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ πρόσωπον) and addressing objections about the body and will. The voice in u01-rem-mid is specifically Adam's person, not Paul's substituted persona generically, and u01-rem-close contains Didymus's own argumentative responses to hypothetical objectors.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὕτω δὴ καὶ τὸν διάβολον οὐ μόνον σατανᾶν καὶ ἀντικείμενον καὶ διάβολον καὶ ὄφιν καὶ λέοντα καλεῖν οἶδεν καὶ Βελίαρ
_unresolved_facts.fix: Add 'ἀντικείμενον' to source_forms, as it appears in the list of names for the devil in u01-open.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The 'flesh,' 'sin,' 'law,' and 'death' that enslave are names for the devil
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὕτω δὴ καὶ τὸν διάβολον οὐ μόνον σατανᾶν καὶ ἀντικείμενον καὶ διάβολον καὶ ὄφιν καὶ λέοντα καλεῖν οἶδεν καὶ Βελίαρ, ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ σάρκα καὶ νόμον καὶ ἁμαρτίαν καὶ θάνατον
_unresolved_facts.fix: Didymus says Scripture calls the devil by these names, but he distinguishes: 'flesh' can mean the devil (ὁμωνύμως, 'homonymously'), but he explicitly denies that Paul attacks the literal flesh 'which we wear' (τὴν σάρκα ἣν περικείμεθα). The 'law' that is sin's law is distinguished from the 'propadeutic' law that punishes sinners. The claim oversimplifies by saying these 'are names for the devil' without the nuance that they are homonymous uses.

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-early move: 'begins a brief commentary on the persona's words, starting with sin using the commandment to deceive'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πειράσω δὴ διὰ βραχέων καὶ εἰς αὐτὰ τὰ ῥήματα τὰ κατὰ προσωποποιΐαν εἰρημένα παρατρεχόντως εἰπεῖν, ἀρξάμενος ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀφορμὴν δὲ λαβοῦσα ἡ ἁμαρτία
_unresolved_facts.fix: Didymus does not 'begin' with sin using the commandment in u01-rem-early; he first argues that the persona's words don't fit Paul or baptized believers, then quotes Rom 8:1-2 about freedom in Christ, and only then (marked by 'Πειράσω δὴ') says he will 'briefly and cursorily' address the persona's words starting with 'sin took occasion by the commandment.' The outline should note this structural sequence more precisely.
